heading: Rivers, bison and country food
intro: Indigenous peoples in Treaty 6, across Alberta and across Inuit Nunangat hold detailed knowledge of the water, plants and animals that ecosystems depend on. That knowledge sits alongside the science of this lab: water cycles, matter cycles and food webs. These connections show some of what that looks like here in Edmonton, across Alberta and across Canada.

connections.title: kisiskâciwani-sîpiy: the river that feeds Edmonton
connections.text: The river that supplies Edmonton's drinking water has Indigenous names. The City of Edmonton says its English name comes from the Cree word kis-is-ska-tche-wan, meaning "swift current," and that the Blackfoot called it Omaka-ty, meaning Big River. The Canadian Heritage Rivers System writes the names as kisiskâciwani-sîpiy and Omaka-ty, and says the river remains a place for ceremony, gathering of medicines and subsistence. Former Chief Jerome Morin of Enoch Cree Nation says: "We've always had an affinity to the rivers, to the lakes, for transportation, for fishing, hunting trapping." The City also says the Cree called this area Amiskwaciy, Beaver Hills. Look for the beaver in this lab's food web.

sources.title: City of Edmonton Archives: Before it was Edmonton

connections.title: Bison return to Banff
connections.text: In 2017, Parks Canada moved 16 plains bison from Elk Island National Park to Banff National Park. By 2024 the herd had grown to over 130. Parks Canada says much of the project's success is due to weaving Indigenous ceremonies and cultural knowledge with western science. Partners include the Stoney Nakoda Nations, Siksika, Piikani, Kainai and Tsuut'ina Nations, Samson Cree Nation and the Rocky View Métis District of the Otipemisiwak Métis Government. Bison are a keystone species. Their grazing and wallowing create habitat, and moving herds spread nutrients through the ecosystem. In the 2014 Buffalo Treaty, signing nations say buffalo "has been our relative."

sources.title: Parks Canada: Plains bison reintroduction, Banff National Park
Parks Canada: The Buffalo: A Treaty of Cooperation, Renewal, and Restoration (2014)

connections.title: Country food and Arctic food webs
connections.text: Inuit have lived on the land, marine waters and islands of the Arctic for more than four thousand years. Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami (ITK) says country foods from the land are central to Inuit culture and way of life. ITK's Arctic wildlife guide calls Arctic char "a favourite food of our people," describes caribou as one of the most important food sources for Inuit in Canada, and says Elders call seal a "special food." It also records food web links: beluga whales feed on Arctic char, and polar bears depend on ringed seals. ITK calls for valuing Inuit wildlife management decision-making and supporting harvesting and sharing systems.

sources.title: Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami: Inuit Nunangat Food Security Strategy

try: Parks Canada says plains bison were nearly extinct over 140 years ago, and that one result was reduced biodiversity. Use what you learned about food webs to predict what changes when bison return to a grassy meadow. Which living things might increase, and why?

Parks Canada says moving bison herds spread nutrients through the ecosystem. Draw a matter cycle that shows how carbon and nutrients in grass could end up back in the soil after a bison eats it. Where do decomposers fit?

ITK's wildlife guide notes that beluga whales eat Arctic char and polar bears depend on ringed seals. Build a short Arctic food chain from these links. Name the trophic level of each animal, and explain why there are far fewer polar bears than seals.

review_flags: Existing lab content (Lesson on the water cycle, and the runoff diagram): the note that Edmonton's drinking water comes from the North Saskatchewan and flows east through Treaty 6 territory is accurate but has no citation in the lab. The Canadian Heritage Rivers System page supports that the river is tied to Treaty No. 6 ("both at Fort Carlton and Fort Pitt in 1876 and also the Adhesion at Fort Edmonton in 1877"). Should I add that page as the note's source? No other Indigenous content was found in the lab or the deck.

Names and spellings: the City of Edmonton Archives page gives the Cree word as kis-is-ska-tche-wan and the area name as Amiskwaciy (fort: amiskwacîwâskahikan), while the Canadian Heritage Rivers System gives kisiskâciwani-sîpiy. I used each spelling only with its own source. Which spelling do you want in the slide point? Also, the sources say "Blackfoot"; I added Niitsitapi in the peoples field following your naming list. Keep it, or match the sources?

The Banff bison partner list comes from Parks Canada, not from the nations themselves. Would you like me to look for each nation's own statement, or a Knowledge Keeper's published words, before this goes to students? I did not describe the ceremonies Parks Canada mentions, on purpose.

The ITK Arctic Wildlife document is older: its nutrition fact sheets are dated March 1996, though ITK still hosts it. It is Inuit-authored and specific about animals, which the newer Food Security Strategy page is not. Is an older ITK source acceptable, or should I keep looking for a current ITK or regional Inuit source (for example Qikiqtani Inuit Association) on country food?
